notes.meaning: The Lord tells the people to search every street and public square in Jerusalem. If they can find even one person who does what is fair and seeks the truth, He will spare the entire city. God is showing that the town is completely corrupt, yet He is still eager to show mercy if anyone truly turns to Him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Older Catholic translations like the Douay-Rheims translate the Hebrew for 'truth' as 'faith,' emphasizing that God was seeking someone with genuine faith.

notes.meaning: The people often took formal oaths by saying, 'As the Lord lives.' Even though they used God's name, their promises were dishonest. Their religious words were just an empty cover for lying and cheating.

God looks at the heart and values genuine honesty. He sent hard times to correct the people, but they refused to learn or feel sorrow for their sins. Instead of repenting, which means turning away from wrongdoing back to God, they hardened their hearts like stone.

Jeremiah wondered if only the poor and uneducated acted so foolishly. He thought they might be breaking God's laws simply because no one had taught them any better. He hoped the problem was just a lack of schooling rather than willful rebellion.

Jeremiah decided to speak to the leaders and rulers, expecting that educated people would respect God's laws. Instead, he found that the wealthy leaders were just as rebellious. Like oxen smashing their wooden neck-harnesses, they threw off all moral restraint.

Because the people refused to obey God, fierce enemies would attack them like wild beasts. Lions, desert wolves, and leopards picture the terrifying speed and cruelty of the invading Babylonian army. Turning away from God left them completely unprotected.

God asks how He can excuse a people who have walked away from Him to worship lifeless idols. He gave them everything they needed to thrive, but they repaid His kindness with betrayal. They even practiced sexual sin at pagan shrines instead of remaining loyal to the Lord.

The men of the city acted like well-fed, wild stallions driven by pure appetite. They chased after their neighbors' wives without any shame or self-control. Their material comfort only fed their selfish desires.

The Lord asks if such blatant sin can be ignored without punishment. As a holy and fair Judge, He must hold a corrupt nation accountable. His justice demands that evil deeds meet their proper consequence.

God commands the enemy army to march through the vineyards of Judah and strip away its branches. The people are compared to vines that no longer produce good fruit for the Lord. Even in this fierce judgment, God orders the invaders not to destroy the root, preserving a small remnant.

Both the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah broke their sacred promises to God. They showed complete treachery toward the Lord who had loved them. Their betrayal was deep and widespread across the entire nation.

The people told lies about God by claiming He would never punish them. They convinced themselves that war and starvation would never touch their homes. They treated the Lord as if He were powerless or indifferent to their wicked deeds.

The scoffers mocked God's true messengers, calling them full of empty wind. They claimed the prophets did not speak for God and wished that the threatened disasters would fall on the prophets instead. Mocking God's warnings only sealed their own ruin.

Because the people laughed at His warnings, the Lord told Jeremiah that His message would act like a consuming blaze. The spoken words would not vanish into thin air like wind. Instead, the words would burn like fire, and the stubborn people would be burned like dry wood.

God announces that an ancient, powerful empire will march against Judah from far away. This refers to the Babylonians, who spoke an unfamiliar foreign language. Because Judah could not understand their speech, they would find no chance to reason or plead for mercy.
The arrow-cases of the Babylonian archers are described as open graves. Their warriors were deadly and rarely missed their targets. Every arrow they fired brought death to someone in Judah.

The invaders would strip the land bare, eating the crops and livestock meant for Judah's families. They would kill the youth and batter down the stone-walled cities that the people trusted for safety. False security in human walls cannot stand against God's decree.

Even during this terrible invasion, the Lord promises not to wipe out His people completely. He leaves a doorway of hope open for the future. God remains faithful to His covenant promises even when He must discipline His children.

When the exiles asked why God allowed such misery, Jeremiah was to tell them the truth plainly. The punishment matched their sin exactly. Because they served foreign gods in their own land, they would now be forced to serve foreign masters in a distant country.

God commands this warning to be shouted throughout the entire family of Jacob and the cities of Judah. No corner of the land was to be left without hearing the message. The warning was urgent and meant for everyone.

The Lord calls the people foolish and blind because they refused to use their senses. They had working eyes and ears, but they closed their minds to God's truth. Deliberate sin had destroyed their common sense and moral judgment.

God reminds them of His mighty power over nature. He placed simple sand as a boundary for the ocean, and the roaring waves stop where He tells them to stop. The powerful sea obeys its Creator, but His own people foolishly dared to rebel against Him.

Unlike the ocean, the people of Judah had stubborn and rebellious hearts. They refused to stay within the boundaries God had set for their lives. Instead, they walked away from Him and kept wandering deeper into sin.

The people never stopped to thank the Lord, who sends autumn rains for planting and spring rains to ripen crops. He faithfully guarded the seven weeks of harvest time so they would have food. Forgetting the Giver of daily blessings led them into proud self-reliance.

differ.view: Some Baptists see the autumn and spring rains as a spiritual picture of the Holy Spirit's refreshing work, bringing revival to the church and preparing believers for heaven.

notes.meaning: Their own sins had disrupted the seasons and held back God's good gifts. When droughts and bad harvests came, it was not because God lacked kindness, but because their rebellion blocked His blessings. Sin always costs people the good things God wants them to enjoy.

Wicked men operated freely among God's people. Like bird hunters hiding in the bushes with nets, they laid clever traps to cheat and ruin their neighbors. They treated human lives like prey to be captured for profit.

Just as a hunter's cage is crammed full of captured birds, the houses of these rich men were packed with stolen goods. They used dishonest business practices and lies to build their fortunes. Their great wealth was proof of their corruption, not of God's favor.

These corrupt leaders lived in luxury, growing fat and comfortable while ignoring the poor. When orphans and needy people came to court for justice, the judges refused to defend them. Their cruelty and greed went far beyond even pagan standards.

The Lord repeats His warning that such injustice cannot go unpunished. A holy God cannot overlook the oppression of the weak and fatherless. He will certainly step in to settle the account with a corrupt nation.

Jeremiah declares that something shocking and horrifying has taken place in the land of Judah. It was so appalling that it was hard to believe it could happen among God's chosen people. The spiritual rot had reached the very core of the nation.

The prophets told pleasant lies, and the priests ruled corruptly by teaming up with them. Worst of all, the ordinary people loved these easy lies because no one rebuked their sins. The Lord asks what they will do when the inevitable day of judgment finally arrives.
